questions.question: Explain why the Soviet Union was a fragile union by the 1980s.
questions.expected_answer: Fifteen republics (Russia largest; Ukraine, Belarus, Baltic states, Caucasus, Central Asia), nearly 290 million people of over 100 nationalities. Formally each republic had rights, but power lay with the Communist Party in Moscow; Russification; Stalin's deportations and the Holodomor; the Baltic states annexed in 1940 after the Nazi-Soviet pact. It was held together by the Party, army and KGB rather than free choice, so it was vulnerable when the centre weakened.

questions.question: Describe the crisis of 1989 to 1991 that weakened the Soviet Union.
questions.expected_answer: Glasnost allowed nationalist movements: the Baltic Way (23 August 1989, about two million people), Lithuania's independence declaration (11 March 1990), Vilnius killings (January 1991, 14 dead), ethnic conflict (Nagorno-Karabakh). Perestroika broke central planning without a market: shortages, inflation, rationing, miners' strikes. The Party lost its monopoly (1990); Yeltsin was elected President of Russia (June 1991); the March 1991 referendum (about 76% yes, six republics boycotting) and a new union treaty due on 20 August 1991.

questions.question: Explain the August 1991 coup and how it led to the end of the Soviet Union in December 1991.
questions.expected_answer: Hardliners (Yanayev, Kryuchkov, Yazov) held Gorbachev at Foros and declared an emergency on 19 August 1991. Yeltsin stood on a tank at the White House; crowds built barricades; troops refused to attack; three died; the coup collapsed on 21 August. The Party was discredited (Gorbachev resigned as General Secretary on 24 August). Republics declared independence; Ukraine voted over 90% for independence (1 December); Belovezha Accords (8 December) created the CIS; Gorbachev resigned (25 December 1991), and fifteen states replaced the USSR. The USA became the only superpower; South Africa's negotiations (CODESA, December 1991) were helped.
